description: The complete guide to Hyoukan — a free, open-source manga and novel reader for Android.
headings: A reader that takes rendering seriously
Books are first-class, not image strips
AI that can stay on the device
text: Android 8.0+ · Apache-2.0 · v1.25.3 Every kind of story,one shelf. Hyoukan is a free, open-source manga and novel reader for Android. It reads image chapters through a hardware-accelerated WebGPU renderer, opens EPUB books as real books, organises a library of thousands, and can translate and upscale pages entirely on your device — with no account and no content hosted by the app. Get started Feature tour GitHub 13tracker services 150+achievements 2readers: comics & books 0bytes of content hosted #Start here 🚀 Getting started Install the app, add sources, build a library and take your first backup. 🧩 Sources & extensions How the extension ecosystem works, which sources are built in, and how installers differ. 📖 Reading comics Pager, webtoon and vertical modes, the WebGPU renderer, gestures and reading settings. 📚 Reading books EPUB and web-novel reading with publisher typography, highlights, footnotes and read-aloud. #What Hyoukan is Hyoukan is a reader, not a catalogue. It does not host, index or distribute manga, novels or images. It displays content fetched by extensions — small APK packages installed separately, exactly as in Tachiyomi, Mihon and Komikku — or content you already own: local folders, CBZ/CBR archives, EPUB files and a self-hosted Komga server. The app is a fork with a long lineage: Hyoukan keeps the entire Mihon and TachiyomiSY feature set, carries Komikku's additions, and adds its own work across the reader, the library, translation, upscaling, books, tracking, backup and diagnostics. It is licensed under Apache-2.0; the source lives at PineappleTwilight/hyoukan. Note A note on names. The project was previously published as Houri and before that as Komikku. The repository and update channels now use the Hyoukan name. The Android application ID is still so existing installs, backups and library databases continue to resolve; that identifier is an implementation detail, not the product name. #What sets it apart #A reader that takes rendering seriously The WebGPU reader is the default on supported devices: HDR pages at full brightness, LUT colour grading, ArtCNN upscaling, dual-page spreads and a memory budget that follows the device rather than a fixed RAM class. When a GPU device genuinely cannot run it, the app falls back to the standard viewer and remembers why. #Books are first-class, not image strips Drop an into a library folder and it opens as a book: the publisher's typography survives, illustrations and fonts travel inside the page, chapters flow continuously or turn as pages, positions survive font changes, and highlights, footnotes and text-to-speech are built in. #AI that can stay on the device Translation runs through a hybrid pipeline — on-device detection, OCR and inpainting, then a cloud LLM, Gemini Nano or a bundled llama.cpp model. Upscaling is a separate pipeline with Real-CUGAN, Real-ESRGAN, Waifu2x and imported ONNX models, and it works even in builds without the translation engine. #A library that stays organised Hierarchical categories, a home-screen-style folder layout, smart categories bound to tracker status, per-category reader settings and update schedules, duplicate detection, merging, migration and a feed that watches sources for you. #Explore the wiki 🌐 AI translation The pipeline, providers, models, glossaries and cache — and what stays on-device. 🔍 AI upscaling Models, backends, per-category defaults, prefetching and the WebGPU tile sampler. 💾 Backup & sync What a backup contains, how restore streams it, and how SyncYomi, WebDAV and Drive work. 🏗️ For developers Modules, DI, navigation, the reader internals, the extension API and the build pipeline. 🧭 Tutorials Guided walkthroughs: translate a chapter, upscale a series, typeset an EPUB, automate the library and calibrate the reader. #Current status Item Value Latest stable 1.25.3 (4 November 2026) Beta channel Published from every push as Minimum Android 8.0 (API 26) Target / compile SDK 36 / 37 Language Kotlin 2.x, JVM target 17 Licence Apache-2.0 See Versions & channels for the full release-channel and signing picture, and Project history for how the fork got here. Warning Hyoukan's developers have no affiliation with any content provider. The app hosts zero content. You are responsible for how you use it and for the content you access.

title: Getting started
description: Install Hyoukan, add sources, build a library and take your first backup.
text: Hyoukan is distributed as an Android APK. There is no Play Store listing; the project publishes signed builds on GitHub, and the app can update itself from the same channel. #Requirements Requirement Detail Android 8.0 (API 26) or newer Architecture recommended. , and builds also ship Storage The app is large because of its native libraries; allow a few hundred MB plus whatever you download Network Needed for online sources, sync and extension installation; local reading works offline Optional A WebGPU-capable GPU for the high-quality reader; 3 GB+ RAM for AI translation; Vulkan or an NPU for the fastest upscaling Note The no-MTL ( ) build omits the translation engine and the bundled llama.cpp runtime. Reading, downloads, tracking, books and upscaling all still work. Choose it if you want a smaller APK or your device cannot run the translation stack. #Install Open the latest release on the device. Download the APK that matches the device's architecture — most phones want . Open the file. Android will ask you to allow installs from that app or browser; accept, then install. Launch Hyoukan. If Android blocks the install with "app not installed", the usual causes are a conflicting signature from an older fork, insufficient free space, or a package installer restriction from the manufacturer. Uninstall the older copy after taking a backup if you are switching from a differently signed build. #Stable and beta Channel Source Notes Stable GitHub Releases on Tagged versions such as Beta The beta repository named by the app's updater ( at the time of writing) Published from every push as ; minified preview builds Beta builds have a different application ID, signing key and update channel. Moving from stable to beta (or back) is a one-time manual install; the two can coexist, but they do not share a library database. The in-app updater is under More → About → Check for updates. Update checks use the channel the installed build was compiled for. #First launch The onboarding flow covers the essentials and nothing else: Theme — light, dark, system, or one of the named colour schemes. Storage — choose the folder used for downloads, backups and the local source. Permissions — notifications, battery-optimisation exemption and, if you plan to use the legacy installers, install unknown apps. Guides — a short tour of where things live. Achievements — opt in only after onboarding. Nothing unlocks before you explicitly decide to have them. After onboarding you land on an empty Library. Tip You can re-run the onboarding guide later from More → Settings → Advanced → Onboarding guide. It explains the interface without wiping anything. #Add sources Hyoukan itself ships with only a few sources: Local source — folders and archives on your device. E-Hentai / ExHentai — 36 language-specific source IDs, with login, favourites sync and metadata. Komga — a built-in client for a self-hosted Komga server. Everything else comes from extensions. To install some: Go to Browse → Extensions. Open the store manager (the ⚙ or "Extension stores" row). Add the URL of a repository you trust and confirm. Browse the store, install the extensions you want, and grant the install permission the chosen installer needs. The Private installer is recommended: it needs no install permission and verifies each extension against the repository's signing key. Shizuku also works without the per-app install prompt. The legacy and package-installer modes go through Android's normal install UI. Important Extensions are third-party software. They can see the sites they connect to and the credentials you enter into them. Install extensions from repositories you trust, and read Sources & extensions before adding an unknown store. #Find something to read Browse a source: Browse → Sources → (source) → Browse, then search or page through the catalogue. Global search searches every enabled source at once from the Browse tab. Add to library from a series page. Choose categories, and optionally fetch metadata and chapters immediately. Local content: put folders or archives in the local source directory and refresh Browse → Sources → Local source. Your library is the centre of the app: it aggregates chapters, download state, tracking, reading progress and categories. See Library & categories. #Take a backup now Before you invest hours in a library, create a backup: More → Settings → Data and storage → Create backup. Choose a location and what to include. For a first backup, keep the defaults: library entries, categories, chapters, tracking, history, settings, extension stores, source settings and custom covers. Optionally enable Automatic backup frequency (hourly to weekly; the app keeps the four most recent automatic backups). Backups are files. They contain your library database and settings, not the downloaded manga pages or the extension APKs themselves. See Backup & sync for the full contents and restore rules. description: Every major Hyoukan feature, grouped by the job it does.
text: This page is the map. Each section links to the guide that covers the feature in depth. #Reading comics Feature What it does WebGPU renderer Hardware-accelerated page rendering with tiled decoding, smooth transitions and memory-aware scaling. Default on supported devices. Pager modes Left-to-right, right-to-left and vertical paged reading, with configurable tap zones and page-turn animations. Webtoon / long strip Continuous vertical scrolling with page splitting, side padding, smart scaling and optional gaps. Dual-page spreads Two pages side by side with deterministic height matching, inversion and a centre margin for foldables. HDR pages PQ, HLG and UltraHDR content at full brightness with clean SDR tone-mapping. Colour grading Brightness, contrast, HLG exposure, built-in LUT presets and custom / madVR files. Smart dark mode Darkens pages on dark backgrounds without destroying line art. E-ink preset Grayscale, boosted contrast, calm transitions and tiled-refresh handling for e-ink panels. Auto webtoon detection Switches to the continuous viewer for entries that look like long strips. Page splitting Pages too tall for the decoder are cut into segments and stitched back into the reading flow. Preload control Separate pages-ahead and pages-behind counts, plus memory-gated prefetch. Reader cache A configurable image cache, with aggressive whole-chapter loading as an option. ArtCNN On-GPU super-resolution for zoomed tiles when the device supports it. Unsharp sharpening A live 0–200% unsharp mask for soft or downscaled scans, WebGPU only (on ). Filter presets Named looks covering brightness, contrast, sharpening, LUT and e-ink, reapplied in one tap (on ). Cutout support Draw into the display cutout area, with per-viewer behaviour. Chapter transitions Optional transition pages between chapters, with a "always show" override. In-chapter search Search the open book chapter as you type, with context snippets and jump-to-match. Chapter completion sound Optional randomized 60/30/10 audio when a chapter finishes, with user sound packs. → Reading comics · Tutorial: calibrate the reader #Reading books Feature What it does EPUB 2 and EPUB 3 Parses and , the OPF manifest/spine, , and both series conventions. FB2 and TXT Local FB2 sections and TXT paragraphs become book pages, with find-in-book; conversion stays on the device (on ). Publisher typography Drop caps, ruby, tables, vertical writing and the book's own stylesheets survive because the reader is a WebView, not a text widget. Books in the library An in a library folder is detected as a BOOK; art books can stay COMIC. Per-entry "Render as book / comic" survives updates. Continuous reading Sections append ahead and prepend behind, so a book scrolls like the continuous manga viewer. Paged and double-page CSS multi-column pagination with page-turn animations, including a spine-swing transition. Table of contents The book's own ToC, indented like a printed contents page and opened at the reader's place. In-chapter search Case-insensitive search with selectable context and a jump to the match. Typography Font size and scale, family (bundled, generic or imported font files), colours with contrast derivation, line/paragraph/letter/word spacing, outline, margins, justification, hyphenation, indentation and vertical writing as follow-book tri-states. Imported fonts Any , , or from storage, validated before acceptance and stored privately. Ignore publisher styles Drops the book's stylesheets so the reader's typography wins on books that hardcode sizes. Force dark A palette rewrite, not a filter: classed backgrounds are neutralised and illustrations keep their colours. Highlights Four pen colours, persistent per chapter, re-marked after reflow, tap to remove. Selection actions Copy and look-up through the system browser, ColorDict or GoldenDict. Footnote popups Tapping a labelled note reference shows the note beside the text, even when it lives in another file. Read-aloud System TTS in document order, chaining across the book and turning pages itself. Auto-scroll Continuous auto-scroll at a chosen dp/s, pausing on touch; timed page turns in paged mode. Status line Clock, chapter progress, chapter name and battery, each toggleable, top or bottom. Custom CSS and JavaScript Reader-authored styles and scripts injected into every document, with JS off by default. Stable positions Reading position is a character offset plus document URL, not a page index. Cover page The declared cover is prepended as page zero when the spine does not already show it. DRM detection DRM-locked books are reported instead of rendered as garbage; font obfuscation is ignored. → Reading books · Tutorial: typeset an EPUB #Library and organisation Feature What it does Hierarchical categories Categories can contain subcategories, with an optional home-screen-style folder layout and a virtual "All" view. text: #The basics #What is Hyoukan? A free, open-source manga and novel reader for Android. It organises a library, fetches chapters through installable extensions or local files, and renders them with either an image reader or an EPUB reader. It does not host or distribute any content. #Is it legal? The application is legal open-source software. What you read with it is your responsibility, and the developers have no affiliation with any content provider. The app hosts zero content and ships no sources beyond the local source, E-Hentai/ExHentai and Komga. #Is it free? Are there ads or subscriptions? Yes, free. There are no ads, no subscriptions and no paywalled features. Optional services you connect — trackers, cloud LLM providers, a Komga server — have their own terms. #Does it collect data? By default, no telemetry is compiled in. Builds made with include Firebase Crashlytics; the official release APKs do not. Logs stay on the device unless you explicitly share them, and translation/upscaling can run entirely on-device. #Why is the package ID still ? The project was renamed from Houri to Hyoukan. Changing the Android application ID would break upgrades, backups and every existing library database, so the ID stays as a stable internal identifier. The product name, repository and documentation use Hyoukan. #Compatibility #What Android version do I need? Android 8.0 (API 26) or newer. The app targets API 36 and compiles against API 37. #Which architectures are supported? , , and . The WebGPU reader runs on 32-bit too, with a deliberately smaller memory budget. The local LLM runtime is 64-bit only for GPU offload; 32-bit devices fall back to CPU inference. #Does it support Android TV? There is no TV-specific interface. It can run on some Android TV devices, but navigation is designed for touch and the app is not tested there. #Can I use an SD card? Yes for downloads and backups through Android's storage access framework. The database lives in app-private storage and cannot be moved to removable media. #Can I import my Mihon, Komikku or Tachiyomi library? Yes. Restore a backup from Settings → Data and storage → Restore backup. Install missing extensions and log back into trackers afterwards. Mihon-format backups (which carry no per-entry update schedule) are supported; the app recomputes the schedule from the backup's chapter list. #Can I go back to an older version? Only by uninstalling the newer build first, which erases app data. Take a backup before downgrading, and expect the database schema of the newer build to be unreadable by older versions. In practice, downgrading usually means restoring a backup made on the older version. #Will stable and beta installs share data? No. They have different application IDs and signing keys. They can coexist, but each has its own library and settings. #Sources and extensions #Why are sources separate extensions? Because the sites change constantly and the app should not ship a hundred scrapers. Extensions are independent APKs: they can be updated without an app release, and the app's core does not need to know about any particular site. This is the same model Tachiyomi and Mihon use. #Why did MangaDex disappear? The in-app MangaDex client, login, follows sync and recommendations were removed. MangaDex remains available through the community MangaDex extension. Removed-source library entries are kept, and their metadata stays readable. #Why can't I install an extension? The usual causes: No extension store is configured. Add a repository URL first. Android has not granted the installer permission. The Private installer needs none; the legacy/package installers do. Android 14+ blocks unverified installs from the app until the per-app "allow" cooldown expires. The Private installer avoids this. The APK is for a different app signature or a newer API level than the device supports. #Are all extensions safe? No one can guarantee that. Extensions are third-party code and can read what they request. Prefer well-known repositories, use the Private installer (which verifies repository signatures), and avoid extensions from unknown sources. #Why does an extension show an error? Most extension errors mean the site changed and the extension has not caught up. Open the extension's details: the app names the repository and offers a GitHub issue search. Updating the extension often fixes it. Cloudflare challenges and rate limits are logged but are not treated as extension failures. #Reading #Why did the reader fall back to the standard viewer? The WebGPU viewer declines for four reasons, in order: the high-quality switch is off; this build recorded two degraded sessions; the GPU device could not initialise or was lost; or constructing the viewer threw. Each reason is written to the in-app log. Turning the high-quality switch off and on clears the health latch and retries. #Why is my page blank or black? description: Step-by-step walkthroughs for Hyoukan's advanced features — translation, upscaling, typography, automation and display tuning.
text: The rest of this wiki explains how each feature works. A tutorial is different: it takes one job, assumes almost nothing, and walks it end to end with a way to check the result. Pick the outcome you want. Tutorial Time You need What you end up with Translate a chapter 15–20 min Internet, a cloud API key or a MangaTranslator account A chapter that reads in your language, cached and tuned to the series Translate fully offline 30–45 min plus downloads A 3 GB+ device and several GB of free storage Translation that never sends a page anywhere Upscale a series 20 min A low-resolution series and a Vulkan- or NNAPI-capable device Sharper pages, with the right model and factor for your hardware Typeset an EPUB 15 min An EPUB in the library A book that looks like a printed page instead of a web page Library on autopilot 20 min A library with entries in categories Updates, downloads, cleanup and tracker sync that run without you Calibrate the reader 15 min A WebGPU-capable device Correct brightness, HDR handling and a LUT that suits your panel #How to read a tutorial Each one follows the same shape: What you'll build — the finished state in one paragraph. Before you start — build, hardware and storage requirements. Steps — numbered, with the exact screen path for every setting. Check it worked — observable results, not "it should work". If something goes wrong — the failures people actually hit. Tip Settings names in tutorials match the English interface. If the app is in another language, the paths are the same but the labels are translated. #Before any tutorial Know your build. The standard build ships the on-device translation engine. The build omits it and translates only through the remote MangaTranslator service; upscaling, books and everything else still work. Know your device. Translation wants 3 GB of RAM and an or build. Upscaling is fastest with Vulkan or an NNAPI NPU, and falls back to CPU and then simple resampling. Have a backup. None of these tutorials touch your library data, but a backup before a large download or a provider change is cheap: More → Settings → Data and storage → Create backup. #The reference behind the tutorials AI translation — the pipeline, providers, models and cache in full. AI upscaling — model families, backends, plan chains and cache identity. Reading books — every typography control and how positions survive reflow. Downloads & storage — the queue, automatic downloads and cleanup rules. Settings index — the screen-by-screen map of every setting mentioned here.

text: This tutorial sets up AI translation (internally MTL) for one series and translates a chapter. It uses a cloud provider because that is the shortest path to a good result; the fully offline tutorial covers local models. Time 15–20 minutes Needs Internet, the standard (MTL) build, and an API key for Gemini, OpenRouter or another supported provider — or a MangaTranslator account Ends with A translated chapter on disk, a prompt policy that fits the series, and a cache that makes the second read instant #What you'll build Hyoukan detects the text on each page, reads it, translates it, erases the original glyphs and typesets the translation into the artwork. The translated page replaces the original in the reader. Once the series is opted in, opening a chapter is all you do; translation runs page by page while you read. #Before you start Check Where Expected Build has the engine More → Settings → AI translation A status row and a Models & engine row. A build says "No-MTL build — enable MangaTranslator for off-device translation" Enough RAM The same screen No "This device has too little RAM" warning (the local pipeline is gated at 3 GB) Free space Settings → Data and storage → Storage usage Room for cached translations; a few hundred MB is usually enough per large series A target language — Decide what language you want to read in before tuning prompts Note In the standard build, even a cloud provider still uses the on-device detector, OCR and inpainter. The cloud part is the language model. In a build, MangaTranslator does the whole page remotely; every other provider is unavailable. #Step 1 — Turn the engine on Open More → Settings → AI translation. Turn on AI Translation. The status row now reports the engine, the selected provider, the model and its readiness. Typical readiness values are "ready", "no model yet", "API key missing", "logged in" and "anonymous". The per-series toggle on the details page stays hidden until this master switch is on. #Step 2 — Choose where the translation happens Open Settings → AI translation → Provider setup → Provider. Provider Account Best for MangaTranslator (remote) None for anonymous use; an ichigo.moe / mangatranslator.ai account for a larger quota The fastest setup, and the only provider in a build Gemini Google AI Studio API key A simple key and vision-aware translation OpenRouter OpenRouter API key Choosing among many models and comparing their wording OpenCode Zen API key An alternative hosted cloud NVIDIA NIM API key An alternative hosted cloud Custom OpenAI Base URL + optional headers + key A self-hosted or proxied OpenAI-compatible endpoint Local (On-device LLM) None Full offline operation — see the offline tutorial Pick one and stay on this screen. #Step 3 — Add the credential and model #Cloud LLM (Gemini, OpenRouter, OpenCode Zen, NVIDIA NIM) Create a key in the provider's console. For example: Google AI Studio for Gemini, or for OpenRouter. Paste it into API key. The row shows only the first four characters once saved. Tap Fetch available models. If the fetch fails, the app falls back to a built-in list; the error is shown on the row. Choose a model. Use a current general-purpose or vision model; very small models translate dialogue poorly. For Custom OpenAI, also fill Custom API Base URL (for example ) and Custom Headers if the endpoint needs them. Keys and model choices are stored per provider, so switching from Gemini to OpenRouter later does not overwrite the first configuration. #MangaTranslator (remote) Choose MangaTranslator (remote) as the provider. On first selection the app turns AI Translation on for you. Open Account — MangaTranslator / ichigo.moe. Sign in, or close the sheet and stay anonymous. Anonymous use is rate-limited; a signed-in account raises the quota. The app stores a session token, never your password. The engine, model and prompt controls are hidden for this provider because it returns a finished image instead of text. #Step 4 — Set the language and the look Back on Settings → AI translation: Setting What to choose Target language The language you read in. Changing it re-translates pages instead of reusing the old language Translation font A font whose glyphs cover the target language. The default is fine for Latin scripts; pick a bundled CJK family for Japanese or Chinese output Text colour Usually black or white, matching the page. A custom hex value is accepted #Step 5 — Opt the series in Open the series from the library. On its details page, turn on Translate Manga. This switch is per entry and off by default. With it off, the reader shows the original pages even though the engine is on. Important Translation uploads page images to the cloud provider you chose. The app gates translation while Incognito or Censor lewd manga is active, so pages are not sent in those modes. #Step 6 — Translate the first chapter Open a chapter and read normally. A chip at the bottom of the reader reports the pipeline: Chip Meaning Translating… 3/18 pages

text: This tutorial configures on-device translation: the detector, OCR model, inpainter and language model all run on the phone. It is the privacy-preserving path and the one that works on a plane. Time 30–45 minutes, dominated by downloads Needs A 3 GB+ device, an (recommended) build, and several GB of free storage Ends with A local translation stack that works in airplane mode, with a model that fits the device #What you'll build The full pipeline — detect → OCR → group → translate → inpaint → typeset — runs locally. Local GGUF models do the language step; the engine models do everything else. Once configured, selecting Local (On-device LLM) as the provider means translation generates no network traffic at all. #Before you start Check Where Expected Standard MTL build Settings → AI translation Local model controls are not hidden and the screen does not say "No-MTL build" RAM The same screen No low-RAM warning. Local LLMs are offered by what the device can actually load Storage Settings → Data and storage → Storage usage Several GB free: engine models plus one local LLM 64-bit ABI More → About → tap the version to copy device info gets the Vulkan build of llama.cpp; 32-bit falls back to CPU Note The local engine models and the local LLM are separate downloads. The engine models (detector, OCR, inpainter) are a few hundred MB; a local LLM is usually one to several GB. Both are required for the fully offline path. #Step 1 — Choose the offline path There are two genuinely offline language models in Hyoukan, plus a hybrid arrangement. Path What it uses Choose it when Local GGUF Bundled llama.cpp with a downloaded or imported model You want full control and the most consistent offline behaviour Gemini Nano Android ML Kit GenAI / AICore The device supports it (for example Pixel 8+ or Galaxy S24+) and you want a smaller download Hybrid Local GGUF for translation, Gemini Nano as a second on-device model You want a fallback that is still offline Gemini Nano availability depends on the device and on AICore finishing provisioning. Local GGUF works on any device that passes the RAM gate, so it is the safer choice when portability matters. #Step 2 — Point the provider at the device Open More → Settings → AI translation. Turn on AI Translation. Open Provider setup → Provider and choose Local (On-device LLM). The cloud-only rows disappear: there is no API key or cloud model to configure. The local model controls live under Models & engine. #Step 3 — Download the engine models Open Settings → AI translation → Models & engine. Tap Download AI models. Wait for the detector (DBNet), OCR and inpainter (AOT-GAN) downloads to finish. The row reports a percentage and the installed size. If you read English or another Latin-script source, also install Install multilingual OCR add-on (PP-OCRv5, about 16 MB). Japanese and Chinese pages are read by the base OCR model; Latin scripts need the add-on. Tip The download is staged and only accepted when complete. If it is interrupted, start it again; a partial file is not treated as a working model. #Step 4 — Get a local language model Under Models & engine → Local (On-device LLM): Open Local model. Auto resolves to the best model the device can load. Read the subtitle: quality tier, parameter count, vision support, translation fine-tune and download size. Tap Download model and wait. The row shows percentage, MB downloaded, speed and an ETA; Cancel download stops it. To use a model you already have: Tap Import GGUF from device. Pick a file. It is copied into private storage and appears in the model list. Select it under Local model. Imported models are treated like built-in ones, but you manage their deletion yourself. #Which model to pick Priority Choice Best translation quality A larger model marked TL finetune, if the device can load it Balanced The Auto pick — the catalog chooses by available RAM Vision-aware pages A model marked vision, with its mmproj available; it can see the page image as context Lowest storage / fastest The smallest model that still produces readable dialogue; expect more literal phrasing Bigger is not automatically better on a phone. A model that does not fit stays in RAM at the expense of the reader and the rest of the system. #Step 5 — Start the engine In the same group, tap Start engine. The subtitle changes from "Stopped" to "Running — (model)". Turn on Start engine on app launch. This preloads the model so the first page of a chapter does not wait for a cold start. If the runtime is missing (a build), the row says Runtime not bundled and no local model can run. #Step 6 — Set the language and opt the series in Back on Settings → AI translation, set Target language. Pick a Translation font that covers the target script. Open a series, and turn on Translate Manga on its details page. Open a chapter. text: This tutorial takes one EPUB from its publisher's defaults to a deliberate page: a font you chose, a measure that fits the screen, justified text with hyphenation, and colours that survive night reading. That is good by default and occasionally bad when a book hardcodes paper-sized margins or tiny type. The tutorial teaches both: a house style for most books, and the escape hatches for the ones that fight it. #Before you start Check Where Expected The book is in the library Library Tapping it opens the book reader, not the comic viewer Reading appearance is reachable Settings → Book reading → Reading appearance The typography sheet opens; it is also in the reader's settings while a book is open Optional font is on the device Files app A , , or file; imports are validated and copied into private storage #Step 1 — Get the book into the library Open Settings → Book reading → Import books. Pick one or more EPUB files. Give the destination folder a name — this becomes the series name. Confirm. The books are copied into a new folder in the local source and appear as one series. For an existing folder of books, put it in the local source instead and refresh the source. A folder whose chapters are all EPUBs is detected as a book. A mixed folder stays a comic. If a title is detected wrongly, open the entry's menu and choose Render as book (or Render as comic); the choice survives library updates. #Step 2 — Choose how the book moves Open the book, then open reading appearance from the reader's settings sheet (or from Settings → Book reading → Reading appearance). Device fonts uses the system's generic families. Add a font… imports your own file. For long-form prose, a serif at a moderate size is the conventional choice; sans-serif reads better on low-density screens and for short sessions. Import a font when you have a specific book face in mind — the import is validated before acceptance, and a family you delete falls back to the default. Then set: Setting What it does Font size The base type size Font scale A second multiplier for the whole page Smooth text Anti-aliasing. Off uses LCD subpixels: sharper on light backgrounds, with colour fringing on coloured text Tip Set Font size first and leave Font scale at its default. Using both to enlarge type makes the relationship between body text and headings harder to reason about. #Step 4 — Set the measure and the rhythm These controls decide whether a page feels typeset or dumped. text: This tutorial wires the library so it keeps itself current: updates run on a schedule, new chapters download before you ask, finished chapters clean themselves up, and progress reaches your tracker without a manual edit. Time 20 minutes Needs A library with entries, at least one category, and (optionally) a tracker login Ends with A repeatable weekly rhythm: update → download → read → sync → clean up #What you'll build Nothing here changes how a page renders. The result is behavioural: fewer taps, less storage drift, and a library that reflects what you are actually reading. #Before you start Check Where Expected Storage location is set Settings → Data and storage → Storage location A valid folder. Downloads cannot start without it Battery optimisation is off for Hyoukan Settings → Advanced → Disable battery optimization Scheduled work is allowed to run A backup exists Settings → Data and storage → Create backup A recent file Tracker (optional) Settings → Tracking → Trackers At least one service logged in, or an enhanced tracker discovered #Step 1 — Build the shelves first Automation follows categories, so the categories have to mean something. Open More → Categories (or Settings → Library → Edit categories). Create shelves you will actually use — for example Reading, On hold, Completed, Scans, Webtoons. Nest subcategories where it helps. A category is a label, not a folder; an entry can be in several. For each category, open its settings and set Update interval. Leave it on Use the global setting unless that shelf needs a different rhythm. A category can also pin a reading mode and orientation for everything on it. That is how a webtoon shelf opens in continuous mode without per-entry fiddling. #Make status shelves move themselves A smart category is bound to a tracker status. When an entry's status changes on a tracker — or you finish the first chapter of something in Wish to read — it moves into the matching category. Only categories you explicitly bind are touched. The move is one-way and idempotent; it never removes an entry from unrelated shelves. Unbound categories are never modified. This is the difference between a category you maintain and a shelf that stays current. #Step 2 — Schedule updates Open Settings → Library → Global update. A category with no interval follows the global one. Tip Leave Launch global updates off once every shelf has an interval. The category schedule then does the work, and a cold start is not spent refreshing the whole library. #Step 3 — Decide what downloads itself Open Settings → Downloads. text: This tutorial tunes the image reader for one screen. It covers the WebGPU renderer's colour pipeline, not the library or source settings: how a page is toned, graded and sharpened before it reaches your eyes. Time 15 minutes Needs A WebGPU-capable device for the full set; the legacy viewer still reads pages without it Ends with A reference page that looks right in daylight and at night, and a LUT you can turn down instead of removing #What you'll build The reader decodes pages into GPU textures, tiles them, and draws them through a render pipeline. On top of that pipeline sit brightness, contrast, sharpening, HDR tone mapping, smart dark mode and LUT colour grading, alongside two other ways to make pages sharper: ArtCNN tile refinement and the AI upscaler. The goal is a stable setup you do not have to revisit for every series. #Before you start Check Where Expected WebGPU is allowed Settings → Advanced → Reader → Use high quality renderer (WebGPU) On. It is the default on supported devices The reader uses it Open a chapter, then Settings → Reader → WebGPU The WebGPU group is present and its settings take effect A test page Any colour page with both dark and light areas Use the same page for every comparison A second test page A night scene or a page with near-black art Reveals crushed shadows #Step 1 — Confirm which renderer is running The WebGPU viewer is not a skin over the old viewer; it is a separate render path. It declines in a fixed order: Use high quality renderer is off. The build recorded two degraded sessions on this device. The renderer cannot initialise or lost its GPU device. Constructing the viewer threw. Every decline writes a line to the in-app log beginning or . If the reader looks like the old viewer, check Settings → Advanced → View logs for those lines before changing colour settings that are not being used. To clear the health latch, turn the WebGPU switch off and on again. A new app build clears it automatically; a single recovered device loss does not count as degraded. #Step 2 — Start from a neutral picture Before grading, make the base display correct. Set Background colour (black, grey, white or automatic) to what you actually read against. Turn on Fullscreen if the system bars are distracting. Open the test page and adjust Brightness and then Contrast: Brightness shifts the whole page up or down. Contrast stretches tones around mid-gray. Both apply live with no re-decode, so compare on the same page rather than reopening the chapter. The WebGPU brightness slider bottoms out at −70%: lower values used to clamp every colour channel to black. A stored value at or below −50% writes a warning to the in-app log. Tip Set brightness before contrast. Raising contrast first makes the brightness control feel wrong, and you end up with a crushed page that needs a second correction. #Step 3 — Tune night reading Under Settings → Reader → WebGPU: Setting What it does Starting point Dark mode filter Smart-inverts pages: white becomes black, art stays readable On at night, off in daylight True black (AMOLED) Crushes near-blacks to pure black to save OLED power On for OLED, off for LCD Gray tolerance How much colour a pixel may carry and still count as grey Raise to catch tinted paper; lower to protect coloured art Color dimming How much kept colours are darkened Raise for night reading; lower if art looks muddy The filter is not a simple inversion. Grey tolerance decides what counts as page paper, and colour dimming decides how much of the remaining colour survives. If a colour page turns into a negative, grey tolerance is too high; if white speech bubbles stay blinding, it is too low. #Step 4 — Handle HDR pages The renderer displays PQ, HLG and UltraHDR content at full brightness and tone-maps the rest to SDR. Setting Effect HLG tone mapping A hybrid log-gamma pass for HDR-ish pages; applies live HLG exposure An exposure shift in EV applied before the HLG curve Brightness / Contrast Global, and still applied after the HDR path If an HDR page looks washed out, adjust HLG exposure before touching global contrast. If SDR pages look fine and only HDR pages look wrong, the HLG pass is the control that matters. #Step 5 — Grade with a LUT A LUT is a colour table applied to the page. Presets are built in; custom files are supported. Set Color LUT preset to Grayscale, Sepia, Warm, Cool or Custom file. Adjust LUT intensity. Lower blends toward the original page; higher applies the table fully. For a custom look, set Custom LUT file to the full path of a or madVR file. It is parsed off the main thread. A light touch is usually right: Warm at moderate intensity takes the blue cast off a cheap panel; Grayscale is for focus, not for e-ink (use the e-ink preset for that). Note The LUT is display-side grading. It does not modify the stored page, the upscale cache or the translation output. Compare translation still shows the original page through the same display pipeline. #Step 6 — Use the e-ink preset on an e

title: Sources & extensions
description: How Hyoukan gets content — built-in sources, the extension ecosystem, installers and diagnostics.
text: Hyoukan separates the reader from the places content comes from. A source is a small program that knows how to browse a site and return entries, chapters and pages. Most sources are not in the app; they are installed separately as extension APKs. #Built-in sources Only a handful of sources ship inside the app: Source What it is Local source Reads folders, CBZ/CBR archives and EPUB files on the device E-Hentai / ExHentai The full E-Hentai client, with 36 language-specific source IDs Komga A built-in client for a self-hosted Komga server Everything else — MangaDex, Mangadex-style aggregators, scanlation sites, webtoon sites — comes from extensions. Note MangaDex is no longer bundled. Its in-app client, login, follows sync and recommendations were removed. Install the community MangaDex extension instead. Library entries from the removed source are retained and their metadata stays readable; MDList tracker rows are cleaned up on upgrade. #The extension model An extension is an Android APK with a specific metadata block and a class implementing the API. The app loads it in a classloader, shows its sources in Browse, and talks to it through a stable ABI. Extensions can be updated independently of the app; this is why the ecosystem survives site changes. Extensions declare: a package name, version code and version name; the app version they target ( and related metadata); one or more sources, each with a name, language, id and optional content warnings; an optional icon. The app never bundles a source's secrets. Login state lives in the source's own preferences, and cookies are stored per source. #Adding an extension store Browse → Extensions. Open Extension stores. Add a repository URL. A repository is a JSON index (commonly ) that lists extensions, their APK URLs and their icons. Return to Extensions and refresh. A store can be disabled or deleted without uninstalling the extensions it provided. Extension updates are matched by package name and signing key, so a store cannot silently replace another store's extension with a different signature. #Installing extensions Four installers are available under Settings → Advanced → Extensions → Installer: Installer Permission Background updates Notes Private None Yes The recommended choice. Verifies the archive against the repository's signing key, stores it privately and loads it without Android's package installer. No 24-hour unverified-install cooldown. Shizuku Shizuku running Yes Uses Shizuku's shell identity. Skips Play Protect verification for updates, so they register immediately. Legacy Install unknown apps No The classic session installer with the Android install UI. Package installer Install unknown apps No Uses sessions directly. Automatic extension updates can run every 6 or 12 hours, daily or weekly. Only the Private and Shizuku installers can update in the background; the others require the user to confirm each install. If an install fails, the Extensions screen records the reason — signature mismatch, incompatible API level, storage, permission or a package conflict. #Content warnings Extensions are classified Safe, Mixed or NSFW. A single extension can carry more than one label because its sources may differ. Under Settings → Browse → Allowed content warnings you choose which labels you accept; sources whose labels you reject are hidden everywhere, not just in Browse. This replaced the old single "show NSFW sources" switch. Existing settings migrate to the new model, and previously visible sources stay visible. Warning Content warnings are advisory metadata supplied by extensions, not a guarantee. They do not filter content inside an extension that mislabels itself. #Delegated sources Some installed extensions can be served by Hyoukan's own implementation instead of the extension's code. This is called delegation and is enabled under Settings → Advanced → Developer tools → Enable delegated sources. The main case is Komga: when a Komga extension is installed and delegation is on, the app substitutes its built-in Komga source under the extension's source id. Settings, library entries, absolute URLs and tracker links carry over, and EPUB books open in the book reader. The switch is read when the source map is built, so changing it requires a restart. Delegation exists because the app's implementation can do things an extension cannot — notably open an EPUB as a book and download it as a file rather than page images. #Komga Komga is a self-hosted comic/manga/ebook server. Configure it from Browse → Sources → Komga → Settings: Server address — for example . API key — optional, for authenticated servers. Display name — how the source appears in Browse. The source browses libraries, series and books; comics read as image pages, EPUBs open in the book reader, and reading progress syncs through the Komga tracker. title: Novel plugins
description: Sandboxed JavaScript novel sources — installation, the QuickJS sandbox, limits and the author contract.
text: A novel plugin is a single JavaScript file that adds a text source. Plugin sources appear in Browse like ordinary sources, and their chapters open in the book reader. Plugin support is on the current build, not in the stable 1.25.3 release. Warning Plugins are code from wherever you got the file. The sandbox limits what that code can reach, but there is no signature check, repository review or content warning for plugins. Install only files from a source you trust. #Installing a plugin Settings → Advanced → Novel plugins → Import plugin file. Pick a file whose first 40 lines contain an and header. The file is validated but not executed on import; it first runs when you browse with it. The picker accepts any file type, but the stored file must parse as a plugin. The script is capped at 2 MiB; larger files and unreadable files are refused. is 1–64 characters from ; must be non-empty. defaults to , to , and must begin with or . Plugins are stored in app-private . That directory is the source of truth: a file copied there appears without any bookkeeping, and a file removed from disk disappears on the next scan, without a restart. Delete plugin removes the file. Library entries remain but stop updating until the plugin is reinstalled; the same yields the same source id, so reimporting keeps those rows. #The sandbox Every plugin method call runs in a fresh QuickJS context that is closed when the call finishes. The script has no filesystem, database or class access and no direct network API. The only injected object is , with , , , and ; is routed to the same host log. There is no global, no and no DOM. Calls are synchronous. Response bodies are capped at 8 MiB, scripts at 2 MiB, and URLs at 8,192 characters beginning with . Requests go through the app's own HTTP client, so they inherit its cookies, user agent and Cloudflare handling. The URL check is a prefix test, not a host allowlist. #Using a plugin source A plugin implements the same source and text-source contracts as a Kotlin source, so browse, search, library updates, tracking, downloads and the book reader work without special handling. Browse results end when a page returns an empty list. If a plugin is deleted, a stub remains so its library rows still explain themselves. #For plugin authors Declare the header directives, then export methods from : Method Returns , Catalogue entries; is optional Catalogue entries Entry details Chapter list An HTML string or array of HTML strings A catalogue entry needs and a stable ; (an absolute URL), , , and are optional. Calls are synchronous and errors become empty results with a line in the in-app log. These plugins are not LNReader-compatible: there are no async promises and no DOM, so an LNReader plugin needs a rewrite of its source logic. The full author contract lives in in the app repository. #Where to go next Sources & extensions — APK extensions, installers and source health. Reading books — the reader plugin chapters open in. text: The comic reader is a full-screen Activity, not an ordinary app screen: it owns the display, the orientation, the volume keys and the S-Pen remote. Opening a chapter from the library, the Updates tab or a series page enters it. #The reader at a glance Tap the centre to toggle the menu bars. Bottom bar — chapter list, previous/next chapter, slider, and configurable action buttons. Top bar — back, chapter name, page indicator, overflow menu and reader settings. The bottom buttons are configurable in Settings → Reader → Reader bottom buttons. #Reading modes Mode Behaviour Left to right (pager) One page at a time, advancing left to right Right to left (pager) One page at a time, advancing right to left — the usual manga direction Vertical (pager) Paged vertically Webtoon Continuous vertical scroll, page by page Continuous vertical Continuous vertical scroll with no gaps, built for long strips Default Resolves to the entry's or category's configured mode Automatic webtoon detection can switch an entry to the continuous viewer when its pages look like a long strip. The Auto Webtoon Mode setting controls whether this is allowed. The reader can also show a brief overlay of the current mode when it opens, and the tap-zone overlay can be shown on first open. #Pager behaviour Tap zones — left, right, top, bottom and centre, each assignable. Invert tap zones flips left/right for RTL reading. Scale type — fit width, fit height, fit screen, original size or smart fit. Zoom start position — where a zoomed page begins. Crop borders — trims uniform white or black margins before display. Automatically zoom into wide images — fills the screen with wide pages. Disable zoom in — caps zoom at the page's fit scale. Zooming out still works. Double tap to zoom — turns the whole double-tap gesture on or off. Split wide pages — cuts a spread into two pages, with inverted placement for RTL. Rotate wide pages to fit — rotates landscape pages into portrait. #Long strip behaviour Smart scale on wide screens — keeps the strip at a readable width instead of stretching it. Side padding — draws the strip in a narrower, centred column. Long strip with gaps — inserts spacing between pages. Tap scroll by page — a tap scrolls a screenful instead of a page. Menu-hide sensitivity — how much scrolling hides the bars. Pinch to zoom and disable zoom out. Auto webtoon detection and the preserve reading position on read entries option. #The WebGPU renderer On devices that support WebGPU, Hyoukan uses the hardware renderer by default. It is not a skin over the old viewer: pages are decoded into GPU textures, tiled, and drawn by a dedicated render pipeline. #What it adds HDR pages — PQ, HLG and UltraHDR content at full brightness, with SDR tone-mapping for the rest. Colour grading — brightness, contrast and HLG exposure; built-in LUT presets and custom / madVR files with adjustable intensity. Sharpening — an unsharp mask for soft or downscaled scans, 0–200%, applied live without a re-decode. It is WebGPU-only and separate from ArtCNN or AI upscaling. Filter presets — save brightness, contrast, sharpening, LUT and e-ink choices under a name, then reapply all of them in one tap. Smart dark mode — darkens light pages on a dark reader theme without inverting illustrations. E-ink preset — grayscale, contrast boost, calm transitions and full-page refreshes instead of tile ripples. Dual-page spreads — two pages side by side, with deterministic height matching, inversion and a centre margin for foldables. Page transitions — none, normal or fast; separate dual-page animations; a configurable transition animation. ArtCNN — an on-GPU super-resolution pass for zoomed tiles. It is display quality only and uses more battery. Fast rendering — skips the tile cache and draws pages directly: less sharp when zoomed, smoother on weak tablets. WebGPU tile cache — Settings → Advanced → Reader → WebGPU tile cache is on by default; turn it off for a GPU that shows black or flickering pages. PowerVR devices always take the cache-free path. Preload ahead/behind — separate counts, memory-gated. Cutout handling — avoid or draw into the display cutout, with a separate choice for dual pages. The sharpening slider, filter presets, tile-cache switch and the −70% brightness floor are on the current build, not in stable 1.25.3. #Why it might not be used declines, in order, when: Use high quality renderer is off. This build recorded two degraded sessions on the device. The renderer cannot initialise or lost its GPU device. Constructing the viewer threw. Every decline writes a line to the in-app log beginning or . The switch's summary also says when the health latch is active. Turning the switch off and on clears the latch and gives the device a fresh try; a new app build clears it automatically. A session counts as degraded only if it ends with the renderer still

title: Reading books
description: EPUB and web-novel reading — typography, navigation, highlights, footnotes and read-aloud.
headings: What can be read as a book
text: Hyoukan treats text as a first-class reading format. An is not rendered as a stack of screenshots; it is opened as a book, with the publisher's XHTML, stylesheets, fonts and illustrations intact. Tip For a practical setup, see Typeset an EPUB like a printed book: fonts, margins, justification, dark mode and a small custom stylesheet. #What can be read as a book Format How it gets here EPUB 2 Local source, Komga, a text-source extension EPUB 3 Same; contents are read as well as FB2 Local source; chapters, headings, emphasis and verse become reader typography TXT Local source; split into page-sized sections at paragraph boundaries Plain text web novels A source that returns text pages Downloaded EPUBs Stored with the chapter and opened from disk, no network needed FB2 and TXT support is on the current build, not in the stable 1.25.3 release. Nothing is uploaded when either format is read. A book's chapter list is one library chapter per file in the library, but inside the reader the book's own spine is the unit of navigation. A five-hundred-file novel opens immediately because only the current section is read; the rest are loaded as you approach them. DRM-locked books are detected and refused with an explanation. Font obfuscation ( ) is not DRM and is ignored, because the text is still readable. #Getting books into the library #Local files Put a folder of books in the local source directory, or use Settings → Book reading → Import books to copy one or more , or files into a new local-source folder. A folder whose chapters are all books is detected as a book; a mixed folder stays a comic. EPUB detection reads the content, not just the extension — a title page and a copyright leaf look like prose to a shape test. FB2 sections and TXT paragraphs are converted locally; see Files & formats. The import button's description still says "EPUB" even though all three formats are accepted. You can override the type per entry with Render as book / Render as comic. The choice survives library updates and refreshes. #Komga A Komga series that contains EPUBs is listed in full, and each EPUB opens in the book reader. Configure the server under Browse → Sources → Komga → Settings. #Extensions Any extension implementing the interfaces gets the book reader automatically. See Extensions & source API. A sandboxed novel plugin from Settings → Advanced → Novel plugins is a text source too. #Reading modes The book reader has three layouts, chosen in Reading appearance → Page mode: Mode Behaviour Continuous The book scrolls like the continuous manga viewer. The next section is appended before you reach the end, and the previous one is prepended above you. Paged One column per screen, turned like a paper book. Double Two columns per screen — the open spread. Pagination is CSS multi-column inside the same WebView. The body becomes the scroll container, so a vertical-writing or right-to-left book can lay its columns right-to-left and scroll toward negative offsets; the reader exposes a normalised position where forward is always . Page-turn animations (paged mode) are off by default. Choose the page sliding off, a dissolve, or a spine swing, with an adjustable speed. #Navigating a book Table of contents — the book's own ToC, indented like a printed contents page and opened at your current position. Entries pointing at another chapter are shown disabled rather than hidden, so the structure stays visible. Previous / next section — the bottom-bar buttons step the book's own sections; volumes turn only at the ends. Slider — shows progress through the current chapter as a percentage and is draggable to seek. In-chapter search — type to search the open chapter, case-insensitively. Results show context snippets and jump straight to the match. Tap zones — a tap scrolls; at the document's edge it turns the section. Vertical-writing books get the correct axis and tap direction automatically. Long-press an illustration — opens it full-screen with pinch and double-tap zoom, plus Set as cover. The chapter selector in the bottom bar becomes the book's contents list while a book is open. A book is one library chapter, so the ordinary chapter list would show a single row; the book's own ToC is far more useful. #Typography Settings → Book reading → Reading appearance is also available from the reader's own settings sheet while a book is open. #Text Setting Notes Font size and scale Independent size and page scale Font family Generic families, bundled families, or fonts you import Bold text Tri-state: follow the book, on, off. Bolding applies to body text, not headings or emphasis Italic Tri-state Line spacing, paragraph spacing, letter spacing, word spacing Typography controls Paragraph indent Tri-state Margins Page margins, applied to the text column rather than the page frame Justification Tri-state: follow, justify, left-align Hyphenation Tri-state Vertical writing Tri-state; a Japanese light novel stays vertical unless you override it Text outline A

title: Downloads & storage
description: Offline reading, the download queue, chapter cache retention and reclaiming disk space.
text: Downloads are the difference between a reader that needs the network and one that does not. Hyoukan has two separate offline mechanisms: downloaded chapters (explicit, kept until you delete them) and the chapter cache (implicit, evictable, used while reading). #Downloads Download a chapter from: the chapter list (tap the download icon, or select several chapters); the entry's details page; More → Download queue for the live queue. Downloads run in a foreground worker, survive leaving the app, and persist across a full app close — the queue is restored once the extension sources have finished loading. #Queue controls Pause / resume the whole queue. Retry a failed chapter. Cancel a chapter or the queue. Per-chapter progress in the notification and the queue screen. #Download settings Settings → Downloads: Setting Effect Only on Wi-Fi Restrict downloads to Wi-Fi Save as CBZ archive Store each chapter as a single instead of a folder of images Split tall images Cut very long pages for reader performance Concurrent source downloads How many entries download at once Concurrent page downloads How many pages download at once Download threads Pages fetched in parallel within a source Download cache renew interval How often the download index is refreshed; manual means you reindex yourself #Automatic downloads Setting Effect Download new chapters Automatically download chapters fetched by library updates Skip downloading duplicate read chapters Do not re-download a chapter you have already read elsewhere Download ahead Pre-download the next chapters of what you are reading Auto download while reading Download the current and next chapter as you read — only when both are already partially available Excluded categories Entries in these categories are never auto-downloaded, even if they are also in an included category #Deleting after reading Setting Effect Delete chapters after reading Off, after the last read chapter, or the second/third/fourth/fifth to last After reading automatically delete Delete a chapter once it is read Allow deleting bookmarked chapters Whether bookmarks protect a chapter from automatic cleanup #Where downloads live Downloads go under the storage location set in Settings → Data and storage: Include chapter URL hash appends the first six characters of the chapter URL's MD5 to the folder or file name. This avoids collisions when two chapters share a title. Disallow non-ASCII filenames makes downloads compatible with storage that cannot represent Unicode. You then need to rename source and entry folders yourself using lowercase UTF-8 hex escapes; chapter files do not need renaming. Reindex downloads rebuilds the index after you move files or restore a backup. Note The database stores download state, but the files are the source of truth for "what is on disk". Reindex after any external change. #The chapter cache While you read, the reader caches pages it has fetched. The cache is not a download: it is evictable, shared with prefetching, and can be cleared without losing anything you deliberately saved. Settings → Data and storage: Setting Effect Clear chapter cache Delete all cached pages now Clear page preview cache Delete page-preview thumbnails Clear chapter cache on app launch Wipe the cache every time the app starts Chapter cache retention Drop cached chapters once unread for 12 hours to 30 days; default off ("until space is needed") Clear page preview cache Page previews used before a page loads Cached chapters show a live countdown in the Downloaded and cached content screen: "expires in …", "kept until space is needed" or "removed at next sweep". Reading a cached chapter resets its timer. #Reclaiming space Settings → Data and storage → Downloaded and cached content is the place to look when storage is tight: Every download whose entry is not in the library, grouped by source, with chapter count and disk size. Cached chapters, with age and expiry. Per-chapter, per-entry and "delete all shown" actions. Entries whose source extension is gone appear as folders rather than entries. Merge children are excluded, so a merged entry's files are never listed as orphans. Two confirmed cleanup actions also exist: Delete downloads not in library — removes downloaded chapters of entries you have removed. Delete all downloads — wipes every downloaded chapter on the device. Library entries, bookmarks and reading progress are kept; failed downloads go too. Neither action deletes your library entries. To remove an entry itself, use the library. #Storage location Settings → Data and storage → Storage location chooses the root for downloads, automatic backups and the local source. It uses Android's storage access framework, so an SD card or a cloud-provider folder works if the provider implements SAF properly. No storage location set means downloads cannot start. Invalid location is reported rather than silently falling back. Storage usage shows used and free space for the chosen volume. Warning Changing the sto

title: Tracking
description: Connect MyAnimeList, AniList, MangaBaka and ten more services, and keep progress in sync.
text: Tracking connects a library entry to a record on an external service. Hyoukan keeps thirteen tracker integrations, including four "enhanced" trackers that discover a server automatically. #Supported services Service Login Notes MyAnimeList OAuth Manga list, score, status, rereads AniList OAuth Manga list, score, progress, relations Kitsu Credentials Manga list and progress MangaUpdates Credentials Reading list and score Shikimori OAuth Russian manga database Bangumi OAuth Chinese anime/manga database Anime-Planet WebView cookie Search and progress ComicK Credentials Official API, rebuilt from scratch MangaBaka Credentials Full progress sync, including total chapter count Hikka Credentials Ukrainian anime/manga tracker Kavita Enhanced Auto-discovered, no credential dialog Komga Enhanced Auto-discovered, also used for book progress Suwayomi Enhanced Auto-discovered Each service has its own capabilities: reading dates, score, reread count, status, priority. Capabilities are registry-level facts, not user toggles. #Connecting a service More → Settings → Tracking. Choose a service and log in using its auth mode: OAuth opens the service's authorisation page in a browser or WebView and stores the token. Credentials asks for the username and password (or API key) the service requires. WebView cookie opens the site's login page and captures the session cookie. Enhanced services need no login dialog; they are discovered from their server. Return to the list; the row shows "Logged in". Tokens are stored in the tracking preference store. A tracker can be logged out without deleting its records, or with them, depending on Delete tracking records on logout. #Tracking an entry From an entry's details page, open the tracking sheet and choose a service. Search for the matching record, then set: Status — reading, completed, on hold, dropped, plan to read. Score — the service's scale. Chapter progress. Reading dates — start and finish, where supported. Reread count — where supported. The entry then shows the tracker's status and score, and updates flow both ways according to the settings below. #Automatic behaviour Settings → Tracking: Setting Effect Open track menu on adding to library Prompt for a tracker when a new entry is added Update progress after reading Push the chapter number to trackers as you read Update progress when marked as read Push when you mark a chapter read manually Auto sync progress from trackers Pull progress changes made on the service Delete tracking records on logout Wipe scores and statuses on logout; off keeps them for a future re-login Select entries using source metadata Auto-match on a source's tracker links (MangaDex-style) Progress updates are rate-limited and retried. A tracker that is offline does not block reading; the update is queued and applied later. #Enhanced trackers Kavita, Komga and Suwayomi are enhanced trackers. They are recognised from the source/server rather than configured with a username and password: They appear only when the corresponding source is available. Entries are tracked automatically when added to the library. Komga also carries book reading progress, so a novel read in Hyoukan is marked read on the server. Enhanced trackers can be hidden per entry and are included in the tracking sheet like any other service. #Relations and recommendations Trackers that expose relations give the entry page sequel and prequel cards: AniList and MangaBaka relations are read from the tracker. MangaDex can fall back for missing relations when its extension is installed. Web novels route to the browser instead of the reader. Recommendations come from AniList, MyAnimeList (Jikan), MangaUpdates and ComicK, ranked by frequency across the library. The related-mangas row has its own display settings (expanded by default, in overflow, Home button visibility). #Definitive tracker source An entry can be in several categories. When a series needs one canonical tracker record, set a definitive tracker for the entry or its category. The choice is used for status updates and smart-category moves, avoiding a tug-of-war between services. #Rereads Rereading is tracked explicitly: Start a reread from the entry's menu. Reread counts are stored per entry and pushed to trackers that support them. A reread starts progress from the beginning without marking the series unread. Achievements can be earned for rereads (see Achievements). #Smart categories and tracking A category bound to a tracker status becomes a smart category: Finish chapter 1 and the entry leaves Wish to read for Reading. Complete the last chapter and it moves to Completed. Only explicitly bound categories are touched. This works with any tracker that reports status, and is the easiest way to keep a shelf current without manual dragging. The move also runs when a series is completed from the chapter selector or the track info dialog, not only when you change the status by hand. #Troubleshooting Login fails — check the service's status pag

title: Backup & sync
description: Portable .tachibk backups, automatic snapshots, SyncYomi, WebDAV and Google Drive.
text: Hyoukan stores everything in one SQLite database. Keeping that database safe has two parts: backups (portable snapshots you own) and sync (keeping several devices aligned). They are not substitutes for each other. Note Importing another service's export is not a restore. Library imports asks you to match each entry to a source; a restore writes Hyoukan's own snapshot back. #Backups A backup is a file — a protobuf stream containing the library, chapters, categories, history, tracking and selected settings. It is not a copy of the database file, and it does not contain downloaded pages or extension APKs. #Creating one More → Settings → Data and storage → Create backup. Option Default What it includes Library entries On Entries, covers, metadata Chapters On Chapter lists and read state Tracking On Tracker links, scores, statuses History On Reading history Categories On Categories and their hierarchy Non-library settings On Read state for entries not in the library Custom entry info On User-edited metadata Saved searches & feeds On Saved searches and feed definitions Custom covers On The actual cover images, not just references App settings On App preferences Extension stores On Configured repositories Source settings On Per-source preferences (logins included) Private settings Off Settings marked ; may include passwords A backup can also be scoped to selected categories, so you can snapshot one shelf without the rest. Warning Backups can contain sensitive data. With private settings or source settings enabled, they can include stored passwords and cookies. Treat a backup like a password database, not like a screenshot. #Automatic backups Settings → Data and storage → Automatic backup frequency schedules a backup every 1, 3, 6 or 12 hours, daily, every 2 days or weekly. Automatic backups: run only when the battery is not low; are written to the automatic-backup folder (or the chosen storage location); keep the four most recent files; older automatic backups are deleted; never run while a restore is in progress. The screen shows the last automatic backup time. #Restoring Settings → Data and storage → Restore backup. Pick a file, choose what to restore, and confirm. Restore options mirror the backup options: library, categories, app settings, extension stores, source settings and saved searches/feeds. A separate Update library after restore toggle (on by default) runs a full library refresh once the restore finishes; it is a follow-up action, not backup content, so checking only it restores nothing. How restore behaves: The file is streamed. Entries are decoded one at a time and restored in batches, so a large library does not need to fit in memory. A block that declares a length over 64 MiB is refused, so a malformed file cannot demand gigabytes of memory. Entries are classified as new, existing or merged and walked twice; merged entries are written after the ordinary chunks. Each batch runs in one transaction, falling back to per-entry writes if the batch fails. Old Mihon-format backups are readable; entries without an update schedule have one computed from the backup's own chapter list. Missing extensions and logged-out trackers are reported before the restore starts. The "Restoring backup" banner clears when the restore finishes, not when the follow-up refresh does. A restore merges into the existing library rather than replacing it wholesale. Entries are matched by source and URL; categories are remapped by id and name. #Integrity and recovery The app protects the database on its own: A startup quick check runs its integrity pragma on the app's own SQLDelight connection, so it reads the same WAL state the app is writing. A rolling local database backup is refreshed at most once a day; the three most recent are kept. If the quick check fails, the latest local backup is restored automatically. If no backup can be restored, the corrupt file is quarantined (renamed with a suffix) instead of crash-looping forever. This is separate from your backups and lives in app-private storage. It protects against corruption, not against uninstalling the app. #Sync Sync keeps several devices aligned. Configure it under Settings → Data and storage → Sync. Service What it needs Off — SyncYomi A host URL and an API key Google Drive A Google sign-in WebDAV Server URL, username, password and a data folder #What syncs The same content classes as a backup, with one important difference: custom covers are off by default for sync so the images do not ride on every request. Private settings are on by default for sync in the current configuration; turn them off if you do not want credentials leaving the device. #Frequency and triggers Synchronization frequency — every 30 minutes, hourly, every 3/6/12 hours, daily, every 2 days or weekly. Sync triggers — sync on chapter read, on chapter open, on app start and on app resume. Any combination. Sync now — run immediately. Show syncing progress banner — show or hide the banner.
